analysis.one_liner: Lets states open Medicaid to any resident who wants to buy in as a low-cost public option.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced June 12, 2025 with no cosponsors and referred to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let each state decide whether to open its Medicaid program to residents who don't qualify for regular Medicaid and aren't covered elsewhere. People could buy in with premiums capped at 8.5% of family income, with the same federal tax credits and out-of-pocket protections that apply to ACA marketplace plans. It would also give the enhanced federal matching rate to any state that expands Medicaid whenever it does so, raise Medicaid pay for primary care doctors to Medicare levels, and require every state Medicaid program to cover reproductive health care including abortion. It was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and referred to two committees.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed and states opted in, people without affordable coverage — especially those who earn too much for Medicaid but find marketplace plans expensive, or who live in areas with no silver plans sold — would gain access to Medicaid-priced coverage with income-based premiums capped at 8.5% of household income, standard ACA out-of-pocket limits, and federal tax credits. People in the ten states that have not expanded Medicaid would also benefit from the new financial incentive to expand, and Medicaid patients would benefit from Medicare-level pay for primary care, which helps them find doctors who accept their coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: Starting January 1, 2026, residents not already eligible for Medicaid and not enrolled in other coverage could buy into their state's Medicaid plan, but only if their state elects to offer it.

Premiums for buy-in coverage could not exceed 8.5% of family income, and deductibles and copays would be subject to the same limits as ACA marketplace plans; enrollees could use the same federal premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions available for marketplace plans.

States could offer the buy-in through their ACA insurance exchanges and limit enrollment to standard open-enrollment periods, and the federal government would cover 90% of the administrative cost of running the buy-in program.

Any state that expands Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act, no matter how late, would receive the enhanced federal matching rate that early-expanding states got, removing the financial penalty that has kept ten holdout states from expanding.

Medicaid payments for primary care would be raised to Medicare rates, and the guarantee would extend beyond family doctors to obstetricians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, certified nurse-midwives, and community health clinics.
All state Medicaid programs would be required to cover comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care, including abortion services.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would cover 90% of the buy-in program's administrative costs, pay the enhanced Medicaid match to any late-expanding state, and fund $50 million for quality-measure updates; states that opt in would run the program and would owe the federal government half of any premiums collected beyond what they spend on enrollees' care. Private marketplace insurers would lose customers in states that offer the option, and federal and state Medicaid spending would rise from the higher primary care payment floor.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; private insurers in opt-in states

drawbacks.text: Participation is at the option of each state, so the public option would exist only where states choose to offer it, leaving residents of other states without the choice.

Enrollees could owe premiums of up to 8.5% of family income plus deductibles and coinsurance at ACA-plan levels, which is a substantial share of a tight household budget even with federal tax credits and cost-sharing reductions applied.

The bill requires every state Medicaid program to cover comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care including abortion services starting January 1, 2026, a condition applying to all states rather than only those opting into the buy-in, which would face immediate political and legal opposition under long-standing federal restrictions on abortion funding.

Raising Medicaid primary care payments to Medicare rates and extending the 90% enhanced federal match to any state that expands Medicaid, whenever it does so, would increase federal Medicaid spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: in states that opt in, people without affordable coverage would get a plan with capped premiums (no more than 8.5% of family income), standard out-of-pocket limits, and federal tax-credit help, backed by a 90% federal share of administrative costs. The honest costs: the state-by-state design leaves people in states that decline the option without it; the 8.5% premium cap can still be a heavy burden for a family near the ceiling; the permanent 90% match for late-expanding states and the Medicare-rate floor for primary care add federal and state spending; and the nationwide abortion-coverage mandate, whatever its merits, would guarantee a floor fight that a narrow, single-sponsor bill is not positioned to win. The bill's biggest design weakness is not what it does but how little political support it assembled.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees on the same day, and with no other members signing on it has not moved since.

narrative.text: Rep. Kim Schrier introduced the bill on June 12, 2025.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced; neither committee has taken it up since.
The action record shows no hearings, markups, floor votes, or any activity after the initial referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet: the bill simply sits in committee. Health insurers in potential opt-in states are spared a new public competitor for now, and holdout Medicaid states are spared the new federal incentive to expand.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill simply sits unacted upon

for.name: Rep. Kim Schrier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its only sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The only support on record is the Democratic sponsor; with zero cosponsors and no votes, no partisan pattern has formed.

industries.note: In states that opt in, people could buy Medicaid-based coverage instead of a private marketplace plan, taking customers and premium revenue from marketplace insurers. For ordinary people this is the point: a lower-cost alternative to private premiums.

Buy-in enrollees could be enrolled through the same Medicaid managed care contracts states already use, so the companies that administer Medicaid would take on new paying customers whose premiums are subsidized by federal tax credits. Their interest runs alongside the public's here, since more covered people means more revenue with no one losing existing coverage.

industries.industry: Primary care providers (family doctors, OB/GYNs, nurse practitioners, community health clinics)
industries.note: The bill locks in Medicaid payment rates at Medicare levels for primary care, which today often pays far less. Higher rates make it easier for patients to find doctors who accept their coverage.

States gain a permanent 90% federal match if they expand Medicaid and a 90% federal share of buy-in administrative costs, but they take on a new program to operate and may owe the federal government a share of any premiums collected above program costs.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, no cosponsors, no committee action in the months since referral, and a dual referral to two committees, this bill follows the pattern of the large majority of House bills that are introduced, referred, and never heard from again. It would need cosponsors, a committee hearing or markup, and eventual floor scheduling to move, none of which has begun; its abortion-coverage provision would also make passage difficult in the current Congress even if it advanced.
